summary_grc: ὁ Εὐρυσθεὺς τῷ Ἡρακλεῖ ἐπιτάττει τοῦ Νεμέου λέοντος τὴν δορὰν κομίζειν· ὁ δὲ τὸν λέοντα ἄτρωτον ὄντα ἄγχων πνίγει.
summary_en: Apollodorus 2.5.1, lightly adapted: the first labour. An arrow-proof lion, a poor host who waits thirty days to sacrifice either to Zeus the Saviour or to a dead hero, a cave with two mouths, and a king who hides in a bronze jar.
caption_grc: περιθεὶς τὴν χεῖρα τῷ τραχήλῳ κατέσχεν ἄγχων ἕως ἔπνιξε.

original.note: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.1, lightly adapted: one story sentence for each sentence of the original, with a few words cut (the herald's father in the last sentence). Apollodorus wrote in the 1st or 2nd century AD. 'τοῦτο ἀκούσας' at the start refers back to 2.4.12: the Pythia had told Heracles to serve Eurystheus of Tiryns for twelve years and perform the labours he set, and then he would become immortal.

sentences.text: τοῦτο ἀκούσας ὁ Ἡρακλῆς εἰς Τίρυνθα ἦλθε, καὶ τὸ προσταττόμενον ὑπὸ Εὐρυσθέως ἐτέλει.

glosses.value: the Pythia's command (Apollodorus 2.4.12): serve Eurystheus for twelve years and you will become immortal
προστάττω (order) | τὸ προσταττόμενον (what was ordered: present passive participle with the article)

τοῦτο δὲ ζῷον ἦν ἄτρωτον, ἐκ Τυφῶνος γεγεννημένον.

glosses.value: Typhon, the hundred-headed monster who fought Zeus

sentences.text: πορευόμενος οὖν ἐπὶ τὸν λέοντα ἦλθεν εἰς Κλεωνάς, καὶ ξενίζεται παρὰ ἀνδρὶ χερνήτῃ Μολόρχῳ.

glosses.value: ὁ ξένος | ξενίζω (entertain as a guest) | ξενίζεται (is entertained, is a guest: historic present)
a day-labourer, a poor man who works with his hands (χείρ)

sentences.text: καὶ θύειν ἱερεῖον θέλοντι εἰς ἡμέραν ἔφη τηρεῖν τριακοστήν, καὶ ἂν μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς θήρας σῶος ἐπανέλθῃ, Διὶ σωτῆρι θύειν, ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ, τότε ὡς ἥρωι ἐναγίζειν.

glosses.value: (Μολόρχῳ) θύειν ἱερεῖον θέλοντι: to Molorchus, who wanted to sacrifice a victim (θέλω = ἐθέλω)
ἱερός | τὸ ἱερεῖον (a victim for sacrifice)
ἐπί + ἀνά + ἐλθεῖν | ἐπανέλθῃ (return; subjunctive after ἄν = ἐάν)
to a hero, i.e. to a dead man honoured at his tomb (ὁ ἥρως, -ωος)
to make offerings to the dead (burnt whole, at night, for heroes)

sentences.text: εἰς δὲ τὴν Νεμέαν ἀφικόμενος καὶ τὸν λέοντα μαστεύσας ἐτόξευσε τὸ πρῶτον·

ἀμφί (on both sides) + στόμα (mouth) | ἀμφίστομος (with two mouths)
ἐπί + εἰς + ἦλθε | ἐπεισῆλθε (came in upon, attacked)
τίθημι | θέμενος (aorist middle participle: putting it)

Heracles himself sacrificed to Zeus the Saviour instead

sentences.text: Εὐρυσθεὺς δὲ καταπλαγεὶς αὐτοῦ τὴν ἀνδρείαν ἀπεῖπε τὸ λοιπὸν αὐτῷ εἰς τὴν πόλιν εἰσιέναι, δεικνύειν δὲ πρὸ τῶν πυλῶν ἐκέλευε τοὺς ἄθλους.

εἰς + κρύπτω | εἰσκρυβῆναι (to hide in: aorist passive infinitive of purpose)

grammar.md:
**Conditions and ὡς in a story.**

**1. A condition inside reported speech.** Heracles tells Molorchus what to do (ἔφη + infinitive), and the instructions depend on two conditions:

> ἂν μὲν … σῶος ἐπανέλθῃ, Διὶ σωτῆρι θύειν, ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ, τότε ὡς ἥρωι ἐναγίζειν.
> 'If I come back safe from the hunt, (he said) to sacrifice to Zeus the Saviour; but if I die, then to make offerings to me as to a hero.'

ἄν (= ἐάν) + subjunctive is the *future more vivid* protasis (Unit 10). The apodosis is an infinitive because the whole thing is reported after ἔφη. Apollodorus writes ἄν in the first half and ἐάν in the second: both are the same word.

**2. Four jobs of ὡς.**

| in the text | ὡς means |
|---|---|
| ὡς δὲ ἔμαθεν ἄτρωτον ὄντα | when (+ aorist indicative) |
| ὡς ἥρωι ἐναγίζειν | as (to), like |
| ὡς νεκρῷ μέλλοντα … ἐναγίζειν | as (to) someone he believed dead |
| (Unit 7) ὡς ἀποκτενῶν | intending to (+ future participle) |

**3. ἕως 'until'.** κατέσχεν ἄγχων ἕως ἔπνιξε 'he held it, strangling, until he choked it': ἕως + aorist indicative for an actual past event.

**4. Participle after a verb of knowing.** ἔμαθεν ἄτρωτον ὄντα 'he learned that it was invulnerable': indirect statement with the participle (Unit 9).

culture.title: Heroes, gods and the lion of Nemea
culture.md:
Molorchus' choice is a real Greek distinction. Olympian gods received **θυσία**: an animal killed at an altar by day, its bones and fat burnt for the god and the meat eaten by the worshippers (Unit 5). The dead and the **heroes** (ἥρωες), great men and women of the past believed to have power from their tombs, received **ἐναγίσματα**: offerings made at a low hearth or into a pit, often at dusk, and burnt whole. Heracles was the exception: he was honoured in some places as a hero and in others as a god, because in the end he was taken up to Olympus.

Athens had many cults of Heracles; the Athenians who fought at Marathon in 490 camped in his sanctuary there, and the gymnasium of **Kynosarges** outside the walls was his. The labours were everywhere on buildings: the metopes of the temple of Zeus at **Olympia** (about 460 BC) show all twelve, beginning with the young hero standing tired over the dead lion, and the 'Hephaisteion' above the Agora shows nine of them on its east front.

Nemea itself, in the hills between Corinth and Argos, held the **Nemean Games** every two years in honour of Zeus, one of the four great Panhellenic festivals. The victors' crown was of wild celery; one legend said Heracles founded them after he killed the lion.
